components.text: Explain why Christian inheritance, rather than conflict during declining or fragmented authority, made modern freedoms historically indispensable.
Whether Christian inheritance is indispensable rather than one historical setting within which rights emerged.
Show that modern rights have a substantive Christian intellectual source not exhausted by institutional conflict and strategic self-protection.
Whether rights are better explained by institutional conflict than by inherited Christian moral anthropology.
Account for canonical restrictions and their exclusionary reception before treating biblical anthropology as a source of modern equal standing.
Whether biblical anthropology supplies a sufficient historical basis for modern equal social standing.
Show that early Christian sources contain substantial countervailing roles for women and explain their relevance to later equal political standing.
Whether canonical restrictions and exclusionary interpretation make Christianity primarily supportive of gender inequality.
Explain why modern emancipation and suffrage require a Christian intellectual trajectory rather than opportunities for oppressed groups to resist.
Provide a rival mechanism for advances in equality and political rights beyond inherited biblical concepts.
Whether Christianity is the best explanation for the Western intellectual genealogy of universal suffrage and related reforms.
Whether inherited Christian belief best explains modern equality and political rights.
Supply an identifiable Christian legal transmission mechanism for rights that is not reducible to modern material opportunity and protest.
Show a Christian institutional source for rights alongside conflict-driven adoption.
Whether material opportunity and resistance explain rights better than Christian intellectual and legal transmission.
Whether institutional conflict rather than Christian legal development supplied enforceable rights.
Establish whether protection of the weak and impartial care had relevant pre-Christian forms that limit a uniquely Christian origin claim.
Challenge the suggestion that protective rights begin with medieval Christian legal development.
Whether compassion and protection of vulnerable people are distinctively Christian in origin.
Whether protection of the weak and rights discourse originated specifically in Christian legal development.
Explain why pre-Christian protective rules and medicine do not establish the same institutionalized concern for poor and sick people as such.
Whether earlier protective and medical analogues defeat a distinctive Christian genealogy of compassion.
Determine whether unique institutional scaling proves Christian authorship of compassion or only a significant Christian contribution.
Separate the cross's possible motivational influence from the prior existence of compassionate values.
Whether unique Christian institutional scaling establishes Christian authorship of compassion and equal treatment themselves.
Whether Christian narrative generated the underlying compassionate values rather than chiefly institutionalizing them.
Provide a rejection condition that distinguishes genuine Christian inheritance from retrospective association with any Western outcome.
The claim that modern values are historically unthinkable without Christianity requires a discriminating causal standard.
Show why a broad Christian genealogy fails to discriminate when biblical materials can justify opposite historical outcomes.
Test whether retrospective success attribution can distinguish actual Christian causation from available contrary Christian precedents.
An indispensable genealogy must discriminate Christian causal inheritance from outcomes that Christianity could retrospectively justify either way.
Distinctive institutional outcomes require a standard that would not equally Christianize opposite arrangements.
Explain how indispensable Christian genealogy handles comparably Christian pro-slavery and abolitionist camps using the same authorities.
Test whether an emancipatory Christian narrative explains abolition despite contrary Christian mobilization.
Whether Christian participation in abolition establishes an indispensable emancipatory genealogy despite contrary Christian practice.
Assess difficult laws and Christian slavery defenses within the Bible's claimed culminating narrative rather than treating isolated permissions as the final horizon.
Supply a criterion favoring the emancipatory reading over retrospective use of isolated verses.
Whether Christian pro-slavery practice defeats the claim that Christianity's governing narrative is emancipatory.
Whether a principled biblical narrative can discriminate emancipatory interpretation from contrary proof-text use.
Explain why a culminating emancipatory narrative overcomes express biblical permissions for capture, ownership, and regulation of slavery.
Whether Christological culmination adequately accounts for concrete biblical permissions and regulation of slavery.
Show how Christianity could oppose slavery historically through gradual transformation despite scripture lacking immediate universal abolition.
Explain the claimed historical direction despite slavery's return and Christian opposition to abolition.
Whether the absence of explicit biblical abolition and continued regulation defeats Christianity's historical emancipatory role.
Whether Christian pro-slavery history prevents crediting Christianity with abolitionary transformation.
Limit the wider gradual-Christian-transformation inference by distinguishing contribution from completion in a separate modern moral domain.
Test whether reciprocal Christian moral development reaches the modern autonomy principle.
Whether gradual Christian moral development generally suffices to establish authorship of the modern moral principle reached.
Whether an internal Christian trajectory adequately explains modern gender equality and autonomy.
Show that Christian marriage supplies consent and contributes causally to modern individuality and equality despite the reciprocity-autonomy distinction.
Whether Christian mutuality stops short of individual bodily autonomy and an unconditional right to refuse sex.
Challenge the inference that additional non-Christian factors were historically necessary by distinguishing actual genealogy from speculative alternative routes.
Reject counterfactual claims that reforms would have emerged through material or resistance-based routes without Christian inheritance.
Whether additional non-Christian factors were needed to reach modern consent and bodily autonomy.
Whether alternative material routes displace the Christian genealogy found in actual history.
